321 Days

The USS Abraham Lincoln left San Diego last November expecting a routine run through the Pacific. It came home this week after 321 days, nearly 11 months, one of the longest continuous deployments the Navy has seen in years. Somewhere along the way, the routine cruise turned into something else entirely.

Instead of the Pacific, the carrier and its strike group were sent to the Middle East. What followed was 40 days of sustained combat operations: 3,693 combat sorties flown by the aircrews of Carrier Air Wing 9, 450 Tomahawk cruise missiles launched, 77 one-way attack drones brought down, and a maritime blockade to help enforce. Through all of it, not one member of the strike group was lost to enemy action.

On October 7, with the ship back off San Diego and a day from pulling in, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth came aboard to pin a rare distinction on the group: the Presidential Unit Citation, one of the highest honors an entire unit can earn, and one the military hands out sparingly. It covers everyone in the fight, from the flight deck of the Lincoln to the escorts screening her, including the destroyer USS Frank E. Petersen Jr.

Hegseth's main message to the crew wasn't about the operations at all. It was a request: thank your families for the months they spent waiting.

Then the Lincoln came home.
